title: Columbia Nitrogen Corp. v. Royster Co.
summary: A detailed written sales contract did not justify excluding trade-usage and prior-dealing evidence without asking whether that evidence could reasonably explain or supplement its terms.
notes: 451 F.2d 3 (4th Cir. 1971). The test of admissibility is not whether the contract appears on its face to be complete in every detail, but whether the proffered evidence of course of dealing and trade usage reasonably can be construed as consistent with the express terms; the court also affirmed the district court's rejection of Columbia's antitrust claims.

sections.Parties: Royster, a fertilizer manufacturer, sued Columbia Nitrogen for failing to take phosphate under a supply agreement. Columbia offered commercial evidence to explain the apparent minimum quantity and price obligations.
sections.Material Facts:
Royster built a phosphate plant and agreed in 1966 to sell Columbia a stated minimum of 31,000 tons annually for three years. The contract included a price, a cost-based escalation provision, delivery terms, and a merger clause. When phosphate prices fell sharply, Columbia ordered less than one-tenth of the scheduled first-year quantity. Royster resold the remainder below the contract price.

Columbia offered witnesses to show that, because weather, crops, farming practices, and agricultural policy made demand uncertain, price and quantity figures in the mixed-fertilizer trade were often projections subject to adjustment. It also offered evidence of substantial departures from stated prices and quantities during six years of dealings with Royster, even though Royster had principally been the buyer in those earlier transactions. During negotiation, the parties had rejected both Royster’s proposed payment for each unaccepted ton and Columbia’s proposed market-matching price clause.
sections.Procedural History: The district court excluded the evidence as inconsistent with a complete and unambiguous writing and entered a $750,000 judgment for Royster. The Fourth Circuit vacated and remanded. Its ruling required consideration of the evidence; it did not conclusively establish that Columbia had no minimum-purchase obligation.
sections.Issue: Does facial completeness or a general merger clause bar evidence of trade usage and prior dealings, and could the particular evidence reasonably be construed as consistent with this agreement?
sections.Holding: The broad exclusion was error. Under the UCC, the question is reasonable consistency with express terms, not simply whether the writing appears complete.
sections.Reasoning:
The Code separately permits commercial context to explain or supplement an agreement. A finding that a writing is complete and exclusive restricts additional negotiated terms, but does not automatically exclude trade usage or course of dealing. The contract’s general statement rejecting verbal understandings did not specifically negate those commercial sources.

Several details supported admission. The quantity heading referred to products supplied under the contract. The writing did not address adjustment to a falling market, and its default clause addressed failure to pay for delivered goods rather than failure to take delivery. Rejection of both parties’ proposed protections left questions that evidence of trade and prior dealings could illuminate. The court therefore required an inquiry into the parties’ actual agreement before calculating damages for its breach. The evidence still had to be established and reasonably reconciled with the express terms; a proffer was not itself a final finding in Columbia’s favor.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: This is a major qualification to the idea that a merger clause excludes all outside evidence. The kind of evidence matters: commercial practices have a distinct place in the Code’s account of agreement.

topics.assent: The court seeks the bargain understood in the parties’ commercial setting.
topics.interpretation: Facial completeness does not resolve the meaning and operation of the quantity and price terms.
topics.trade-usage: Usage and six years of dealing could explain the disputed obligations.
topics.parol-evidence: A general merger clause does not automatically negate the UCC’s special treatment of trade usage and course of dealing.
topics.course-dealing: The excluded evidence included the parties' prior course of dealing, in which stated prices and quantities had repeatedly been adjusted.
topics.integration: The court held that a merger clause and apparent completeness do not by themselves exclude usage and course-of-dealing evidence under UCC 2-202.

mnemonic.rationale: Phosphate, and the price of it
